description: Every week a climate headline goes viral: this region is warming fastest, the rain is vanishing. Some are true. Some are noise dressed up as signal. We are putting claims on the stand: NASA satellites are the witnesses, honest statistics cross-examine, and whatever survives leaves with an evidence pack anyone can check. Join us if you love Earth data, maps, clear stats or a good story. Beginners welcome; curiosity is the only requirement.
summary: A teaching prototype: a student can discover how selected years change a headline, and learn why a responsible analysis sometimes cannot give a verdict. Climate Claim on Trial examines specific trend claims for a stated measurement, place and period, using NASA Earth data. Claims are registered first; method changes are disclosed. It tests each trend with a t-test, the Mann-Kendall test with the Sen estimate, then checks those tests on simulated records. These are simulation checks under stated assumptions; the procedure is frozen, not broadly validated. When its checks fail, it withholds a verdict. Withheld describes this tool's limits; it does not establish that the claimed change is absent. Six cases: Alaska air temperature, 1981 to 2025 (reanalysis model output) is supported, up 0.44 degrees C per decade. Sahel rainfall is partly supported (significant under both tests we ran). Wisconsin haze is not supported, though our test is cautious, so that is not proof of no rise. Southeastern US summer land surface temperature and two regional nitrogen dioxide records are withheld; the NO2 readings point the claimed way, but year-to-year memory in a 21-year record defeats every validated test. It runs in the browser: no server, no AI model.
details:
WHAT A STUDENT DOES AND LEARNS

Investigate Earth-system trends with NASA data. A student picks a claim such as "Alaska has warmed", or asks their own question: one of 22 NASA measurements, a place and a range of years. The site draws the yearly record, tests the trend, and shows what changes when you change one thing at a time: the years, the test, the map. The student learns what "significant" means and why a careful test sometimes has to say "we cannot rule on this evidence". The page ends in a ruling: supported, partly supported, not supported, contradicted, or withheld. Withheld describes this tool's limits; it does not establish that the claimed change is absent.

THE PROBLEM

The answer to "has the climate changed where you live?" depends on choices that are rarely shown: measurement, place, years and test. On our home page, one NASA record for interior and western Alaska gives a cooling trend of 0.53 degrees C per decade for 1998 to 2012 and a warming trend of 1.75 for 2005 to 2019; over all 45 years it is about +0.4. We selected these two windows to illustrate how the estimated trend changes with the years. Both describe their selected periods; neither represents the full record.

WHAT WE BUILT

We test each trend with the Sen slope and the Mann-Kendall test, corrected for years that resemble each other. Six registered claims each get a map of every grid cell. The False-Alarm Planet, a made-up world with no trend, shows a plain test flagging 19.3% of cells.

WHAT IS NEW: the tool tests its own tests. Before any verdict it measures each test's false-alarm rate on simulated records like the real one, and when no test passes it says "withheld" instead of guessing. Every claim is registered before its data, and every change is disclosed.

THE SIX CASE FILES (real NASA data; each line gives variable, region, years, source type, and what it cannot establish)

1. Alaska: annual mean 2 m air temperature, interior and western Alaska, 1981 to 2025; MERRA-2 model output, not a measurement. Supported: +0.44 degrees C per decade (95% interval 0.19 to 0.63, p = 0.0015); 85% of the area flagged. Weather-station records show slightly slower warming (see README). It cannot establish a cause; the box includes sea cells.

2. Sahel: June to September rainfall, central Sahel, 2001 to 2025; GPM IMERG satellite estimate. Partly supported: +0.21 mm per day per decade (0.10 to 0.33), significant under both tests we ran: p = 0.030 (plain Mann-Kendall) and p = 0.004 (bootstrap, chosen after we saw the first result; the first was already valid, so the change bought power, not validity). 22% of the area flagged. It stops being significant if consecutive years are even modestly alike (year-to-year memory of 0.2 or more).

3. Southeastern US: June to August daytime land surface temperature, 2001 to 2025; MODIS Terra satellite. Withheld. Its descriptive cooling slope, -0.35 degrees C per decade (p = 0.27), does not establish a broader regional climate trend. No candidate test kept its false alarms near 5% for 25 summers with this much memory.

4. Wisconsin: summer aerosol optical depth (haze), 42 one-degree cells, 2003 to 2025; MODIS Aqua satellite estimate. Not supported: +0.03 per decade (interval -0.013 to 0.079, p = 0.114), none of 42 cells flagged. A plain t-test gives p = 0.04. Our test would catch only about one modest trend in four, so it cannot establish that no rise happened.

5. Eastern US NO2: annual tropospheric NO2 column, 2005 to 2025; OMI on Aura satellite estimate. Claim: it has fallen. Withheld. The record declines (-0.61 x10^15 molecules per square centimeter per decade, for reading only). Our straight-line procedure can mistake a bending trend for year-to-year dependence (memory 0.70, above the 0.6 we tested), so it gives no calibrated finding here.

6. Northern India NO2: annual tropospheric NO2 column, 2005 to 2025; OMI on Aura satellite estimate. Claim: it has risen. Withheld. The slope, +0.36 x10^15, is for reading only. At 21 years and memory 0.39 all seven candidate tests raised too many false alarms.

These NO2 records show opposite trend directions; they do not identify causes, measure surface exposure, or rank countries. Our verdict check cannot handle curved trends: for a simulated clean curved decline like the eastern US record, it gave a verdict in 0 of 2,000 runs. That is a limit of the method, so withholding the verdict is the honest result.

Extra satellite check (exploratory; it changes no ruling): Terra's daytime overpass moved from about 11:00 to 9:47 local time by 2025; it may affect the Southeastern US record, and this check does not show that it did. Aqua's overpass has also drifted later since 2021; we claim no direction for its effect on Wisconsin.

Space agency partner data: ESA Land Surface Temperature CCI (v3.00) is a second record for the Southeastern US case (exploratory; no ruling depends on it).

HOW WE KEPT IT HONEST

- We wrote each claim down and committed it to git before downloading its data: Alaska, Sahel and Southeastern US at 10:29 AM ET on Nov 14, Wisconsin at 10:35 AM ET, and the NO2 pair at 1:15 PM ET.

- We adjusted some test rules after early results and after an outside review, and we show both versions on the site. The last adjustment moved the Sahel result (p 0.030 to 0.004) and Wisconsin (from withheld to not supported).

- The times of those rule changes are recorded in our project log; git alone cannot prove them.

- We publish the checks that failed, and 107 automated tests compare our statistics with the standard Python packages (pymannkendall and SciPy).

Full details: METHODS.md, the README's Limits section, and the site's Method page.

ACCESSIBILITY AND LICENSE

Static files (Python 3.12, plain JavaScript, globe.gl), light and dark themes, keyboard use, a data table behind every chart. Code and text are MIT licensed; the data keep their sources' terms.

LIMITS

- Checks use simulated series only. For Alaska, 7.4% of trendless series that earned a verdict were called significant (4.8% counting withheld ones).

- A ruling does not say why something changed and is not a forecast. Our simulations assume straight-line trends and one-year memory, not long-memory noise, sudden steps, rare extreme years or curved trends.

- More limits (no correction for testing six cases at once, the Sahel map's low sensitivity, region boundaries, and the library checks) are in the README's Limits section.

Independent entry, not endorsed by NASA. No NASA logos; NASA missions and products are named as credit.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) TOOLS

I designed and directed this project and used SI tools as assistants, disclosed here:

- Claude Code (Anthropic): my coding assistant. I set the plan, the claims, the tests and the checks; Claude models generated and tested the data scripts, statistics, web pages and tests under that plan, looked up and summarized sources (linked in the Space Agency Partner & Other Data list), and I reviewed every result. This is LLM-assisted development I directed.

- Codex (OpenAI): while choosing the design, I had Codex sketch the main screen in five themes (editorial, lab notebook, courtroom, mission control, classroom); after comparing the five, I narrowed it down to the courtroom theme. Codex also reviewed plans and results as an outside reviewer, and we fixed what it flagged.

- ElevenLabs: an SI voice clone of my own voice, made with my consent, narrates the 30-second video. I chose the final script from drafts written with Codex's help.

What I decided: the challenge, the claims, regions, periods and test rules (registered before any data download), the design, and every later change, each logged with its time and reason in the repository.

No SI at runtime: no SI model runs on the site; all result sentences come from fixed templates.

Marking: the video narration is an SI voice clone of Walter Guevara (ElevenLabs), made with his consent; the video's last frame and its YouTube description label it "AI voice clone". The screens in the video are recordings of the working site on real NASA data; no image or video in the product or the video was generated by an SI model.

Where the idea came from

Before the event I brainstormed approaches to several challenges, using a language model as a sounding board, and picked this one myself. I then wrote a planning spec and an event schedule. Nothing project-specific was built before the hackathon: the build started on Saturday, November 14 at about 10 AM ET (the first commit is at 10:29 AM ET), and all code, data processing and the final design were done during the event under my direction.

BEFORE THE EVENT

On Nov 5 and 6 I did planning only: research on past winners, a planning spec and schedule, reviews of that plan, and checks of which NASA data catalogues exist. On Nov 12 I wrote generic hackathon templates (theme switch, contrast checker, export and video tools) with nothing about this project in them. No NASA data was downloaded and nothing project-specific was built before the event; the repository's event record shows what was made during it.
